title: Lavender Tallow Balm: The Weird Jar That Fixed My Spring Skin
body:
Okay so I got this thing. A jar of whipped beef tallow balm. Lavender scent. Sounds insane, right? Beef fat. For your face. I ordered it on a Tuesday night, I think. Or maybe it was Wednesday. It was raining. My skin felt like one of those old paper bags, you know the kind. All tight and weird. Spring does that. The air’s all hopeful but your face is just confused. Dry, then oily, then peeling. A mess.

I saw this tallow stuff on Etsy. Some little shop in France. The pictures looked nice. Calming. Said it was for sleep and anxiety. My brain went: “Lavender, good. Beef tallow, what the actual hell.” But I was desperate. And my credit card was just… out. So I clicked buy. Figured it would be a story at least. “Remember that time I put cow fat on my face?” Good party bit.

It showed up like two weeks later. Small brown box. The jar inside was glass. Heavy. Cold from the mailbox. I opened it right there in my kitchen, leaning against the counter. My sock had a hole in it. I remember that.

## How Beef Tallow on Skin Stopped Sounding Crazy

First impression? The smell. Not like a candle. Not like soap. Just… lavender. But real. Like if you crushed the plant in your hand. Not sweet. Herbal. Green almost. I stuck my finger in. The texture was weird. Not bad weird. Thick. Like really thick butter left out on the counter. But then it just… melted. On my finger. No greasy film. It was gone. My skin just drank it. Huh.

So I put it on my face. Because why not. Already bought it.

Here’s where I had to get over myself. Beef tallow. It sounds medieval. Or like something your weird homesteading cousin makes. But then I started poking around. When you’re bored at 11 PM and your face feels like a desert, you Google weird things.

Tallow is basically rendered beef fat. From grass-fed cows. People have used it forever. Like, centuries forever. On skin, on leather, in soap. Grandma wisdom type stuff. It fell out of fashion when big companies started making stuff in labs with long chemical names. But the thing is—and this is the science-y bit I sort of understood—our skin’s natural oil? Sebum? It’s got a lot of similar fats to what’s in tallow. So when you put it on, your skin kinda goes, “Oh, I know this guy.” It recognizes it. It absorbs it. Doesn’t just sit on top like some plastic-y lotion.

It’s not like slathering yourself in bacon grease. That’s lard. Different animal, different fat structure. This is suet fat, whipped with… I don’t know, magic? Until it’s this airy balm. The one I got is from this Etsy shop, Pure Plenitude. They whip it with lavender and some other natural ingredients. No water. No filler. Just the fat and the plants.

So my initial “ew” reaction was just… dumb. It’s just an ingredient. A good one. My face doesn’t care about marketing. It just wants to not hurt.

## What This Lavender Tallow Balm Actually Does

I started using it at night. After I wash my face. I’d scoop a little—it doesn’t take much—warm it between my fingers, and just pat it on. The lavender smell is the main event for that. It’s not a perfume. It’s the actual plant. They say it’s calming. Sleep-promoting. I don’t know if it’s psychosomatic, but the routine itself became the thing. Rubbing this cold, herbal-smelling fat on my face meant the day was over. Brain off.

But the results weren’t in my head. My skin got quiet.

Before, my cheeks were always a little red. Tight. If I smiled too big, it felt like it might crack. After a few days of this tallow balm, that just… stopped. The dryness was gone. But it wasn’t oily. It was just normal. My skin felt like my skin again, not this hostile entity I had to negotiate with every morning.

I used it on my hands too. Because winter had wrecked them. Knuckles all rough. I’d put a blob on the back of one hand, rub them together, and go to bed. Woke up and they were… fine. Not baby soft. Just not painful. No cracks. It fixed my elbows. I didn’t even know my elbows needed fixing, but they were like sandpaper. Now they’re not. Weird.

The benefits of tallow skincare, for me, were just simple. It fixed the dry. It didn’t cause new problems. It’s just intensely moisturizing because it’s basically food for your skin barrier. All those natural ingredients working with your skin, not against it.

## My Skin After a Few Weeks of This Stuff

So it’s been a while now. Spring is actually here. The pollen is trying to kill me, but my face is chill.

I don’t use it every day anymore. Maybe every other night. Or if I’ve been outside in the wind. It’s my fixer. My skin just seems more resilient. I had a spot of eczema on my wrist—this dry, itchy patch that’s been there for months. I started putting the tallow balm on it. Just because. It’s almost gone now. I’m not saying it’s a miracle cure. I’m saying it helped when a lot of other “eczema creams” didn’t.

The jar is still half full. A little goes a long way. It sits on my nightstand next to my water glass and a pile of old receipts. It looks… honest. No crazy claims on the label. Just what it is.

Would I buy it again? I already did. I got one for my mom. She has that super dry, sensitive skin that nothing works on. She called me last week. “What is this witchcraft you sent me?” She loves it. Uses it on her face and her cuticles. She said it smells like her grandmother’s garden. That’s the timeless herbal thing, I guess. It doesn’t smell like a spa. It smells like a plant. And beef fat. But in a good way. You get used to it. Then you like it.

## Quick Questions I Get Asked

**Is beef tallow good for your face?**
Yeah, honestly. It sounds wild but it makes sense once you get past the idea. Our skin produces similar oils. Grass-fed beef tallow is packed with vitamins and fats that help repair the skin barrier. It’s not greasy if you get a good, whipped balm. It just sinks in.

**Does tallow balm clog pores?**
It shouldn’t. In fact, it’s supposed to be non-comedogenic. Because it’s so similar to our own sebum, it absorbs deeply instead of sitting on top and blocking pores. My skin is kinda prone to clogging and this hasn’t caused any issues. It’s actually calmed things down.

**What does lavender tallow balm smell like?**
Not like a candle. It’s a real, earthy, herbal lavender smell. Like crushed leaves. It’s calming. Not sweet or perfumey. It’s strong when you open the jar but fades to a soft scent once it’s on your skin. It’s the main reason I use it at night—just feels like a signal to my brain to shut off.

Anyway. If your skin is being difficult with the season change, or just in general, this might be worth a shot. It’s one of those things that seems too simple to work. But it just… does. I’m probably gonna order another one soon. Just to have around.
